content: 1. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), including the administration of rabies immunoglobulin (RIG), is essential for individuals with category III exposure to rabies. 2. Individuals who have discontinued a PEP series after receiving at least two doses of the rabies vaccine should be considered vaccinated prior to any future exposure. 3. The risk of rabies virus (RABV) infection depends on the type of exposure, the epidemiological context, and the availability of biologicals for PEP. 4. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is recommended for individuals at occupational risk of rabies exposure, such as animal healthcare workers and medical professionals who frequently care for rabies patients. 5. Laboratory workers handling high concentrations of live RABV or lyssavirus should undergo antibody testing every 1–2 years to ensure adequate immune response and mitigate risks from unnoticed exposures. 6. Laboratory supervisors or employers are responsible for assessing exposure risks and monitoring the immunity of laboratory personnel. 7. Serological testing and booster vaccinations are only recommended if the risk of RABV exposure persists. 8. If serological testing is unavailable, routine booster vaccination may be considered before assigning individuals to high-risk positions, but periodic boosters are only advised for those with continuous or frequent exposure risks. 9. Veterinarians and animal health officers not at continuous risk should undergo serological monitoring every two years. 10. PrEP for entire populations is generally not cost-effective but may be considered in remote areas with limited PEP access and high dog bite incidence (>5%) or prevalent vampire bat exposure. 11. PrEP should not detract from mass dog vaccination campaigns, which are critical for controlling rabies at its source. 12. Immunocompromised individuals should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. Those with well-managed conditions, such as HIV patients on antiretroviral therapy, typically respond to rabies vaccines similarly to healthy individuals. 13. In cases of exposure, a complete PEP course, including RIG, should be administered without delay. 14. All bite wounds and scratches should be thoroughly washed with soap and water for at least 15 minutes immediately after exposure. A viricidal agent, if available, should be applied to the wound. 15. Local remedies for wound care are strongly discouraged. 16. RIG should be administered for category III exposures, and wounds requiring suturing should be loosely sutured only after RIG infiltration. 17. Rabies exposure is categorized as follows: Category I: Touching or feeding an animal or licks on intact skin (no PEP required). Category II: Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches, or abrasions without bleeding (PEP with vaccine indicated). Category III: Transdermal bites or scratches, mucous membrane contamination with saliva, or exposure to bats (PEP with vaccine and RIG indicated). 18. The incubation period for rabies is typically 2–3 months, but rare cases may exceed one year. 19. Rabies vaccine should be provided regardless of the time since exposure if the animal is confirmed rabid, even if reported years later. 20. In endemic areas, most domestic animal exposures are not to rabid animals, but risk assessment should be conducted by trained personnel familiar with rabies epidemiology. 21. Integrated bite case management programs can improve detection of RABV exposure, adherence to vaccination recommendations, and reduce unnecessary vaccine or RIG administration. 22. Wildlife acting unusually should be evaluated for rabies risk based on local epidemiology. 23. Human-to-human rabies transmission is extremely rare and has only been documented in cases of organ transplantation and probable perinatal transmission. 24. Rabies virus can theoretically be transmitted through saliva, tears, or nervous tissue, but the risk is low. 25. Rabies transmission through breastfeeding has not been documented, and there is no public health risk associated with it. 26. Rabies transmission through ingestion of raw meat or milk from rabid animals has not been documented, but consumption of such products is not advised. 27. Bites from wild animals, particularly monkeys, should be avoided to reduce unnecessary PEP use. 28. Rabies is rare in rodents, and no human cases from rodent bites have been reported. 29. Inhalation of RABV-containing aerosols is a rare transmission route, primarily in laboratory or cave settings with high bat densities. 30. Prompt local wound treatment is critical in PEP. Wounds should be thoroughly washed with soap and water, and viricidal agents like povidone-iodine should be applied. 31. Bleeding wounds indicate severe exposure and should be infiltrated with RIG. 32. Suturing should be delayed after RIG infiltration to allow immunoglobulin diffusion, and secondary sutures are preferred for better cosmetic outcomes. 33. Infected bite wounds are not a contraindication for RIG administration. 34. RIG can be safely injected into sensitive areas like fingertips, ear lobes, or genitalia, provided excessive pressure is avoided to prevent compression syndromes.
